claims.text: The proposed approach will calculate lattice and electronic thermal conductivity separately in HfNbTaTiZr.
Machine-learned force fields can capture the phonon dynamics and scattering relevant to lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations can determine the electronic thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will predict measured thermal conductivity within 20% over 100–1200 K.
The total thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr is 10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are nearly equal below 200 K in defect-free HfNbTaTiZr.
Spark plasma sintering of gas-atomized powder can produce single-phase random-solid-solution HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed specimens can be prepared with oxygen contamination below 0.12 wt%.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr specimens can be treated as defect-free bulk crystals.
Atomic mass and force-constant fluctuations affect phonon scattering in random alloys.
A simple mass-fluctuation analytical model is insufficient to reproduce all observed phonon-linewidth behavior in a high-entropy alloy.
Local compositional disorder modifies the electronic band structure and thereby influences free-electron heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly separating phonon and electron transport will produce more precise predictions because the channels have different temperature dependences and scattering mechanisms.
Earlier Debye-temperature or linear-mixture approaches conflate lattice and electronic thermal transport.
Earlier approaches show larger deviations from measured HfNbTaTiZr conductivities than the proposed model will show.
The new approach will improve predictive accuracy by roughly 20% relative to earlier models.
Oxygen contamination can prevent formation of a single-phase random solid solution in HfNbTaTiZr.
The model may cease to be applicable above 1 wt% oxygen because of additional defect scattering or phase separation.
Electrical resistivity combined with the Wiedemann–Franz law and phonon spectroscopy can decisively identify separate electronic and lattice conductivity contributions over 100–1200 K.
